# Real-Time Online Tic-Tac-Toe

## Position in the curriculum
Post-course portfolio expansion: build after finishing the full curriculum through the final capstone. This is the catalog's introduction to real-time, bidirectional communication, deliberately started with the simplest possible game so the WebSocket plumbing is the thing being learned, not the game logic.

## Beyond what the lessons taught
WebSockets and Spring's `spring-websocket`/STOMP support are not covered by the 25-chapter curriculum, which teaches request-response HTTP (Chapter 18) and in-process concurrency (Chapter 17) but not a persistent, bidirectional server connection. Treat learning Spring's WebSocket support as required, deliberate self-directed research for this project, using the official Spring Framework reference documentation as your primary source.

## Already-proven foundation
Chapter 17's executor and shared-state material is exactly what protects a game's board state from being corrupted by two moves arriving at nearly the same instant; Chapter 20's State pattern is a good fit for the game's own turn/win/draw state machine, which you have already built once in a simpler form in earlier catalog entries.

## Project scope
A server holds one or more in-memory `GameSession`s, each with a 3x3 board and two connected players. A player connects over a WebSocket, is matched into a session (a simple two-player queue is sufficient; no ranking required), and sends a move; the server validates the move is legal (correct turn, empty cell, game not already over), applies it, and broadcasts the updated board to both connected players. Detect a win or draw server-side and end the session; do not trust a client to declare its own win. Handle a player disconnecting mid-game explicitly (forfeit after a grace period, or pause and allow reconnection — your choice, documented).

## Required evidence
- A concurrency test simulating two near-simultaneous move messages for the same session, confirming exactly one is applied and the other is rejected as "not your turn" or "cell occupied," never both silently applied.
- A full win/draw detection test suite covering every winning line and a genuine draw.
- A test (or documented manual walkthrough) of the disconnect-handling behavior you chose.
- A test confirming an illegal move (wrong turn, occupied cell, game already over) is rejected without corrupting the board state broadcast to the other player.
- A short write-up of your WebSocket message protocol (the shape of a move message and a broadcast update), since no lesson defined one for you.

## Review and completion
A reviewer opens two browser tabs (or two WebSocket client sessions) as the two players, plays a complete game to a win, then starts a second game and has one player disconnect mid-game, expecting your documented disconnect behavior to actually occur rather than the server hanging or crashing.

Design and document a message protocol for a real-time feature no lesson specified
